newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan panel opts against outlawing subway cult.
newsitem.headline: Japan panel opts against outlawing subway cult.

text.p: Japan's Public Security Commission on Friday decided not to invoke a draconian 1952 subversion law to outlaw the religious sect accused of the deadly nerve gas attack on Tokyo subways, officials said.

The independent commission's widely anticipated decision not to apply the Antisubversive Activities Law to Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) rejects a request filed last July by the Justice Ministry's Public Security Investigation Agency.
The harsh law, promulgated during Japan's labour and leftist turmoil after World War Two, was considered so controversial that it had never been applied to a group.

Aum Shinri Kyo founder Shoko Asahara and dozens of his followers are on trial for murder and other charges for the March 1995 sarin nerve gas attack on Tokyo's subway system, which killed 12 people and made thousands ill.
With nearly all senior leaders in police custody and undergoing lengthy trials, cult membership has dwindled from a peak of 10,000 to several hundred.

Asahara was removed from Tokyo District Court on Thursday for disrupting his murder trial. The 41-year-old former yoga teacher ignored pleas by his lawyers to keep quiet and shouted at witnesses and judges presiding over the hearing.
